# How to use this subject

Modern Pharmaceutics (MPH 103T) is the industrial core of the first semester of M.Pharm (Pharmaceutics). It builds on B.Pharm Industrial Pharmacy I (BP502T: preformulation, tablets, parenterals) and Industrial Pharmacy II (BP702T: scale-up, quality management, regulatory). At M.Pharm level examiners expect mechanisms, equations, worked numericals and the guideline behind each practice (ICH Q1A(R2), Q2(R2), Q8–Q10, Schedule M, WHO, US FDA).

## How the units map to the syllabus

The PCI syllabus has five numbered items, with item 1 split into 1(a) and 1(b), each worth 10 hours. These notes follow that split, so there are six units:

| Unit | Syllabus item | Topics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1(a) | Preformulation, drug–excipient interactions, stability kinetics and ICH stability testing, dispersion theory, emulsions, suspensions, SMEDDS, SVP and LVP |
| 2 | 1(b) | Optimization: OFAT vs DoE, factorial, CCD, Box–Behnken, mixture designs, RSM, contour plots, applications |
| 3 | 2 | Validation: VMP, calibration, URS–DQ–IQ–OQ–PQ, types, regulations, dosage-form validation |
| 4 | 3 | cGMP, layout, services, maintenance, production and materials management, inventory, PPC, forecasting, budgets, industrial relations, TQM |
| 5 | 4 | Physics of compression, consolidation, friction, force distribution, compaction profiles, solubility |
| 6 | 5 | Heckel, Kawakita, diffusion, dissolution (f1, f2, Higuchi, Peppas), PK parameters, statistics (SD, t-test, chi-square, ANOVA) |

Study one unit every two days: read the notes, rework every worked example with a calculator without looking, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short (5-mark) and long (10-mark) questions.

## Exam pattern

Theory paper: **100 marks = 25 internal assessment + 75 end-semester examination (3 hours)**. PCI does not prescribe a section pattern for M.Pharm papers, so the mock paper here uses the common PCI B.Pharm 75-mark split, which several universities also use for M.Pharm (for example Bahra University, Shimla). Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

There is also a quick 20-question, 20-minute MCQ test for daily practice.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — appears in most question papers of this kind; prepare a full structured answer with equations, a diagram and a worked number.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a larger question.
- **Low** — rare; useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common question patterns, not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Preformulation parameters, drug–excipient compatibility methods, Arrhenius and shelf life, ICH stability conditions, DLVO and flocculation, SMEDDS, LVP vs SVP |
| 2 | Factorial design with effect calculation, CCD vs Box–Behnken, RSM and contour plots, applications in formulation |
| 3 | Types of validation, URS/DQ/IQ/OQ/PQ, validation master plan, process validation of tablets or parenterals, cleaning validation |
| 4 | cGMP objectives and layout, inventory control (EOQ, ABC), PPC, sales forecasting, TQM |
| 5 | Stages of compression, deformation mechanisms, bonding theories, force distribution and friction, compaction profiles |
| 6 | Heckel plot, f1/f2 calculation, Higuchi and Peppas, PK parameters, t-test, chi-square, ANOVA |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. Open every essay with a crisp definition (and the guideline it comes from), then a labelled diagram or flow chart, then the equation, then applications.
2. Numericals carry easy marks: write the formula, substitute with units, box the answer, add a one-line interpretation ("f2 = 63.9 → similar"). Practise the eight types in this pack: Arrhenius shelf life, factorial effects, Cpk, EOQ, tensile strength, Heckel Py, f1/f2, and t-test/ANOVA.
3. Learn the fixed numbers exactly: ICH conditions (25/60, 30/65, 40/75; India zone IVb 30/75), t90 = 0.105/k, f2 50–100, f1 0–15, BE limits 80.00–125.00%, Peppas n 0.45/0.89 for cylinders, rotatable α 1.414 (k = 2), BBD 15 runs for 3 factors, Six Sigma 3.4 DPMO, Cpk ≥ 1.33.
4. Draw: DLVO energy curve, V-model of qualification, Heckel plot with A, B, C types, force–displacement curve with work areas, contour plot, layout flow of a tablet block, PDCA cycle.
5. For validation and GMP answers, name the regulation (revised Schedule M, 21 CFR 211, EU Annex 15, WHO TRS, ICH Q7–Q10) — postgraduate answers are expected to be regulation-aware.
6. Link topics across units: DoE (Unit 2) builds the design space that validation (Unit 3) confirms; compaction profiles (Unit 5) give the data for Heckel analysis (Unit 6); f2 and ANOVA (Unit 6) are the statistics behind scale-up and post-approval changes.

# Last-night revision sheet

## Unit 1: Preformulation, stability, dispersions, parenterals

- Preformulation = physicochemical + biopharmaceutic profiling before formulation; feeds QbD (CMAs → CQAs).
- Key tests: pKa, S0 and pH–solubility, log P/log D, intrinsic dissolution (Wood's apparatus), polymorphs (DSC, PXRD, TGA), hygroscopicity (DVS), flow (Carr's index, Hausner ratio).
- BCS high solubility: highest single therapeutic dose dissolves in ≤ 250 ml over pH 1.2–6.8 at 37 °C (ICH M9).
- Interactions: Maillard (lactose + amine), magnesium stearate + aspirin, peroxides in povidone/PEG/polysorbate, aldehydes cross-link gelatin. Screens: DSC (fast), isothermal stress testing + HPLC (confirms), FTIR, PXRD, microcalorimetry.
- Kinetics: first-order t½ = 0.693/k, t90 = 0.105/k; zero-order t90 = 0.1C0/k0; suspensions apparent zero order.
- Arrhenius ln k = ln A − Ea/RT. Example: k 0.0042/0.0105/0.0250 day⁻¹ at 50/60/70 °C → Ea ≈ 82 kJ/mol, k25 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ day⁻¹, t90 ≈ 326 days.
- ICH Q1A(R2): long term 25 °C/60% RH or 30 °C/65% RH (12 months); intermediate 30/65; accelerated 40 °C/75% RH (6 months); fridge 5 ± 3 °C. India zone IVb 30 °C/75% RH. Q1B: 1.2 million lux h + 200 W·h/m² UV.
- Significant change: 5% assay change, degradant over limit, dissolution failure, pH failure, appearance failure.
- Emulsion theories: interfacial tension, oriented wedge, interfacial film (mono-, multimolecular, solid particle). DLVO: VT = VA + VR; secondary minimum = loose flocs.
- Suspensions: Stokes v ∝ d²; F = Vu/V0; β = F/F∞; controlled flocculation + structured vehicle.
- HLB blend: 72% Tween 80 + 28% Span 80 for required HLB 12.
- SMEDDS: oil + surfactant (HLB > 12) + co-surfactant; < 100 nm; Pouton types I–IV; pseudo-ternary phase diagram.
- SVP ≤ 100 ml, LVP > 100 ml (USP); no preservative in LVP or intrathecal; 0.9% NaCl ≈ 308 mOsm/L; particulate LVP ≤ 25/ml ≥ 10 µm, ≤ 3/ml ≥ 25 µm.

## Unit 2: Optimization

- OFAT misses interactions. Factors, levels, responses, effects, interactions, aliasing, resolution.
- Screening: Plackett–Burman (N − 1 factors in N runs), fractional factorial, Taguchi.
- Full factorial 2^k; CCD = 2^k + 2k + n0 (13 runs for k = 2 with 5 centre points); rotatable α = (2^k)^¼ = 1.414 (k = 2), 1.682 (k = 3); BBD 15 runs (3 factors).
- Mixture designs: simplex lattice, simplex centroid, extreme vertices; Scheffé model.
- Effect = (Σ+ − Σ−)/2^(k−1); coefficient = effect/2. Example 2³: A +3.45, B −2.35, C +1.85 min.
- 2² example: Y = 84 − 10X1 + 4X2 + 2X1X2 → HPMC 14.5% gives 85% release.
- RSM steps: design → model → ANOVA/lack of fit → contour and 3-D plots → optimum → check-point batches. Desirability 0–1; overlay plot = design space.

## Unit 3: Validation

- Validation = documented evidence of consistency; calibration = traceable to standards; qualification = equipment/facilities.
- VMP: policy, organisation, list and status, schedule, change control, documentation.
- URS → DQ → (FAT/SAT) → IQ → OQ → PQ; V-model pairs.
- Types: prospective, concurrent, retrospective, revalidation. FDA 2011 lifecycle: design → PPQ → CPV.
- Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ; Cpk = min(USL − x̄, x̄ − LSL)/3σ; example Cp 1.39, Cpk 1.22; target ≥ 1.33.
- Cleaning validation: worst case, PDE / 10 ppm / 1/1000 dose criteria, swab and rinse with recovery. Media fills for aseptic processes.
- ICH Q2(R2): specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, LOD 3.3σ/S, LOQ 10σ/S, robustness.
- Regulations: revised Schedule M (Dec 2023), 21 CFR 210/211, EU Annex 15, WHO TRS, PIC/S.

## Unit 4: cGMP and industrial management

- cGMP: no mix-ups, contamination or errors; written procedures; traceability.
- Layout: unidirectional flow; airlocks; pressure cascade; dedicated blocks for penicillins/cytotoxics.
- Maintenance: breakdown, preventive, predictive, TPM; logbooks and status labels.
- ABC (A ≈ 10–20% items, 70–80% value), VED, FSN, HML, SDE.
- EOQ = √(2DS/H) → 1,386 kg in example; ROL = usage × lead time + safety stock = 600 kg.
- PPC: routing, scheduling, loading, dispatching, follow-up.
- Forecasting: moving average 50.3, trend 55.1, exponential smoothing 50.2 (example).
- BEP = fixed cost/(price − variable cost) = 75,000 packs.
- TQM: Deming PDCA, Juran trilogy, Crosby zero defects, Ishikawa fishbone, 7 QC tools, Kaizen, 5S, Six Sigma (3.4 DPMO), ICH Q10.

## Unit 5: Compression and compaction

- Compression (volume ↓) + consolidation (strength ↑) = compaction.
- Stages: rearrangement → elastic/plastic/brittle deformation → bonding → elastic recovery → ejection.
- Plastic (MCC, NaCl): speed- and lubricant-sensitive. Brittle (DCP, sucrose): insensitive. Elastic (paracetamol): capping.
- Bonding: solid bridges (fusion, recrystallisation), intermolecular forces / cold welding, mechanical interlocking.
- σt = 2F/(πDt) → 80 N, 10 × 4 mm = 1.27 MPa. Porosity example 15.1%.
- R = FL/FU (0.85 example); FA = FL + FD; FL = FA e^(−4µKH/D).
- Dwell time 15.5 ms at 30 rpm, 7.8 ms at 60 rpm (410 mm PCD, 10 mm flat). SRS = (Py high − Py low)/Py high.
- Profiles: force–time, force–displacement (net work, plasticity factor E2/(E2 + E3)), radial vs axial, ejection, elastic recovery (5.9% example).

## Unit 6: Parameters and statistics

- Heckel ln[1/(1 − D)] = KP + A; Py = 1/K = 110 MPa (example); DA = 0.548; DB = DA − D0. Types A (plastic, parallel), B (fragmenting, converge), C (no rearrangement).
- Kawakita P/C = P/a + 1/(ab); a = 0.40, 1/b = 33 MPa.
- Fick J = −D dC/dx; P = DK/h; tL = h²/6D → D = 2.3 × 10⁻⁹ cm²/s; P = 0.012 cm/h.
- Release: zero, first, Higuchi Q = kH√t, Hixson–Crowell cube root, Peppas Mt/M∞ = ktⁿ (cylinder 0.45 / 0.89), Weibull.
- f1 = Σ|R − T|/ΣR × 100 (0–15); f2 = 50 log{[1 + (1/n)Σ(R − T)²]^−½ × 100} (50–100); example f1 7.7, f2 63.9.
- DE45 58.2%, MDT 16.5 min (example).
- PK: Cmax 8.1, Tmax 2 h, AUC0–∞ 64.9 µg·h/ml, ke 0.166 h⁻¹, t½ 4.2 h, MRT 6.8 h, Frel 94%. BE: 90% CI 80.00–125.00%.
- Stats: SD uses n − 1; t-test t = 5.00 > 2.228; χ² 4.40 > 3.841; ANOVA F 15.6 > 4.26; p < 0.05 → reject H0.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: investigation of physical, chemical and biopharmaceutical properties of a drug, alone and with excipients, before formulation, so that a stable, bioavailable, manufacturable product is designed with least trial and error; first step of QbD (identifies critical material attributes).
2. Identity and purity: HPLC impurity profile, residual solvents.
3. Solid state: polymorphs, hydrates/solvates, amorphous content by DSC, TGA, PXRD, hot-stage microscopy, FTIR/Raman; metastable forms dissolve faster but may convert.
4. Solution properties: pKa (potentiometric/UV), intrinsic solubility and pH–solubility profile S = S0[1 + 10^(pH − pKa)] for a weak acid; log P/log D (shake flask); salt selection.
5. Intrinsic dissolution rate (fixed-area disc, Wood's apparatus): values below about 0.1 mg/cm²/min suggest dissolution-limited absorption.
6. Stability: pH–rate profile, forced degradation (heat, humidity, acid/base, oxidation, light) to find pathways and develop a stability-indicating method.
7. Powder properties: particle size and shape, bulk/tapped density, Carr's index, Hausner ratio, angle of repose, compressibility (Heckel), hygroscopicity (DVS).
8. Biopharmaceutics: permeability (Caco-2), BCS class.
9. Drug–excipient compatibility: DSC screen, isothermal stress testing with HPLC.
10. Decisions: salt/polymorph, dosage form, process (direct compression vs granulation), excipients, pack and storage label, analytical methods; BCS II drugs → solubility enhancement (solid dispersion, SMEDDS, size reduction).
questions.question: Define preformulation. Describe the preformulation parameters studied for a new drug substance and explain how the results guide formulation design.

questions.answer:
1. Orders: zero order C = C0 − k0t, t90 = 0.1C0/k0; first order ln C = ln C0 − kt, t½ = 0.693/k, t90 = 0.105/k; second order 1/C = 1/C0 + kt.
2. Apparent zero order in suspensions (only dissolved drug degrades; k0 = k1Cs); pseudo-first order for hydrolysis with excess water.
3. Factors: pH (specific and general acid–base catalysis; pH–rate profile gives pH of maximum stability), temperature, ionic strength (log k = log k0 + 1.02zAzB√µ), dielectric constant, moisture, oxygen, light, metal ions, excipients.
4. Arrhenius: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); ln k vs 1/T is linear, slope −Ea/R; extrapolate to storage temperature.
5. Worked example: k = 0.0042, 0.0105, 0.0250 day⁻¹ at 50, 60, 70 °C; slope = −9,890 K → Ea ≈ 82 kJ/mol; ln k25 = −8.04 → k25 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ day⁻¹; t90 = 0.105/k ≈ 326 days.
6. Q10 method: Q10 = k(T+10)/kT, often 2–4; quick estimates.
7. Limitations: mechanism or order may change with temperature; not for physical changes (melting, emulsion cracking, protein denaturation, polymorph change); moisture content varies with temperature in solids; diffusion-controlled solid-state reactions; evaporation of solvent; so real-time data must confirm.
8. Regulatory link: ICH Q1A(R2) accelerated 40 °C/75% RH for 6 months supports, but does not replace, long-term data; shelf life by ICH Q1E statistics.
questions.question: Discuss the kinetics of drug degradation and the use of the Arrhenius equation in predicting shelf life. Add a worked example and the limitations of accelerated stability testing.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: isotropic mixture of oil, surfactant and co-surfactant/co-solvent containing dissolved drug that forms a fine o/w micro-emulsion (droplets usually < 100 nm) spontaneously on gentle agitation in GI fluids; SEDDS give about 100–300 nm droplets.
2. Components: oil (medium-chain triglycerides, mono- and diglycerides, oleic acid); surfactant (HLB > 12: polysorbate 80, polyoxyl castor oil, caprylocaproyl macrogolglycerides); co-surfactant/co-solvent (Transcutol, PEG 400, propylene glycol, ethanol).
3. Mechanism: drug presented in solution; large interfacial area; lipid digestion → mixed micelles with bile; lymphatic transport of lipophilic drugs bypasses first-pass; some surfactants inhibit P-gp and enzymes; less food effect.
4. Pouton classification: type I oils; II oils + water-insoluble surfactants; IIIA/IIIB oils + water-soluble surfactants ± co-solvents; IV surfactants/co-solvents without oil.
5. Development: solubility screening → pseudo-ternary phase diagrams (water titration) → micro-emulsion region → choose ratios → drug loading → optimise by mixture design/DoE.

1. Factorial design: all factors varied together; every combination of levels studied; 2^k runs for k factors at two levels; detects interactions, unlike OFAT.
2. Coding: low −1, high +1; X = (actual − centre)/half range.
3. Example: A binder, B superdisintegrant, C compression force; response disintegration time (min): (1) 4.2, a 7.8, b 2.6, ab 5.0, c 5.9, ac 10.1, bc 3.7, abc 7.3.
4. Effect = (Σ responses at + sign − Σ at − sign)/2^(k−1) = /4. A = (30.2 − 16.4)/4 = +3.45; B = −2.35; C = +1.85; AB = −0.45; AC = +0.45; BC = −0.15; ABC = +0.15; mean 5.825.
5. Interaction column = product of signs of parent columns.
6. Regression coefficients = effect/2: Y = 5.825 + 1.725A − 1.175B + 0.925C − 0.225AB + 0.225AC − 0.075BC.
7. Interpretation: binder lengthens and disintegrant shortens disintegration; force lengthens; interactions small. Prediction A −1, B +1, C −1 = 2.53 min (observed 2.6).
8. Significance: half-normal plot or ANOVA with replicates/centre points; Yates' algorithm as hand method.
9. Fractional factorials (2^(k−p)) for many factors with aliasing; resolution III/IV/V.
10. Advantages: efficiency, interactions, model for prediction; limitation: two levels cannot show curvature (add centre points or move to RSM).

questions.answer:
1. RSM: statistical and mathematical techniques to model a response affected by several factors and find the optimum; uses a second-order model Y = b0 + Σbixi + Σbijxixj + Σbiixi².
2. Steps: screening → choose design → randomised runs → multiple regression → ANOVA (model significant, lack of fit not significant, R², adjusted and predicted R²) → plots → optimum → check-point batches.
3. CCD: 2^k factorial + 2k axial points at ±α + centre points; runs = 2^k + 2k + n0 (13 for k = 2 with 5 centres); rotatable α = (2^k)^¼ (1.414, 1.682); face-centred α = 1 (three levels); five levels when α ≠ 1; can be built sequentially from a factorial.
4. BBD: three levels, mid-edge points + centre; 15 runs for 3 factors, 27 for 4; no extreme corners (useful when corner combinations are impossible); not sequential; fewer runs than CCD for 3 factors.
5. Contour plot: lines of equal response on two factor axes; parallel straight lines = no interaction; curved = interaction/quadratic; ellipses = maximum/minimum; saddle = minimax.
6. Overlay plots of several responses with constraints give the design space; desirability function for multiple responses.
7. Applications: matrix tablets, microspheres, nanoparticles, SMEDDS (with mixture designs), coating and granulation processes, HPLC methods.
8. Validation with check-point batches and percent prediction error.

questions.answer:
1. Optimization: finding best formulation/process within constraints for one or more responses.
2. Parameters: problem type (constrained/unconstrained), variables (independent: formulation and process; dependent: responses), single vs multiple responses.
3. Classification: classical calculus-based; statistical DoE (screening — Plackett–Burman, fractional factorial, Taguchi; factorial; response surface — CCD, BBD, 3^k; mixture — simplex lattice/centroid, extreme vertices); sequential search (EVOP, simplex, steepest ascent); computer search (grid, Lagrangian, canonical analysis, neural networks, genetic algorithms).
4. EVOP: small planned changes (2² around set point) during production, repeated cycles; set point moved when improvement is significant; safe, slow, for production.
5. Simplex: k + 1 vertices; worst vertex reflected through centroid of the rest; Nelder–Mead modification expands/contracts; no model needed; can stop at local optimum.
6. Lagrangian: objective function and constraint equations combined with multiplier λ; partial derivatives set to zero; needs equations (from regression); example maximise dissolution subject to hardness ≥ limit.
7. Grid search: evaluate fitted models over a grid, list feasible points, choose best; handles many constraints.
8. Desirability approach for multiple responses.
9. Advantages of statistical methods over OFAT: interactions, fewer runs, prediction.

1. Validation: documented evidence that a process, procedure, equipment, material or system consistently leads to the expected results. FDA (2011): collection and evaluation of data from process design through commercial production establishing scientific evidence that a process is capable of consistently delivering quality product.
2. Prospective: before commercial distribution; protocol, PPQ batches; batches released after completion; preferred.
3. Concurrent: during routine production with release as data accumulate; only exceptional (low-volume, urgent need) with justification.
4. Retrospective: from historical batch data (10–30 batches); old products only; not acceptable for new products.
5. Revalidation: after changes (formula, equipment, site, supplier, batch size) or periodically; driven by change control and product quality review.
6. Lifecycle: Stage 1 process design (development knowledge, DoE, risk assessment, control strategy); Stage 2 process qualification (facility/equipment qualification + PPQ with heightened sampling; number of batches justified, traditionally three); Stage 3 continued process verification (control charts, capability).
7. Process capability: Cpk = min(USL − x̄, x̄ − LSL)/3σ; example spec 95–105%, mean 100.6, SD 1.2 → Cp 1.39, Cpk 1.22 (target ≥ 1.33).
8. Other validations: cleaning, analytical (ICH Q2(R2)), computerised systems (GAMP 5), equipment qualification.
9. Merits: consistent quality, less rejection/recall, regulatory compliance, reduced testing.

questions.answer:
1. Qualification: documented proof that equipment/facilities are installed correctly, work and give expected results.
2. V-model: URS ↔ PQ; functional specification ↔ OQ; design specification (DQ) ↔ IQ; build, FAT and SAT at the base.
3. URS: user's written needs — capacity, materials (SS 316L contact parts), cleanability, safety, controls, alarms, data integrity (21 CFR Part 11), utilities, documentation, training.
4. DQ: documented verification that the proposed design meets URS and GMP; drawings, P&ID, vendor selection, risk assessment.
5. FAT at vendor, SAT at site.
6. IQ: installed as per design and manufacturer's recommendations — model/serial numbers, component list, materials certificates, utilities, as-built drawings, calibration of critical instruments, manuals, SOP drafts.
7. OQ: functions across anticipated operating ranges — controls, interlocks, alarms, speed/temperature/pressure at limits, power failure recovery; usually without product.
8. PQ: integrated system performs consistently with product/placebo under routine conditions over several runs.
9. Example — HVAC clean room: airflow, air changes, HEPA integrity test, pressure differentials, smoke study, recovery, particle counts at rest and in operation, viable monitoring; water system PQ in three phases over about a year.
10. Requalification after changes/periodically; all under change control and the VMP.

2. Stages: die filling and particle rearrangement → deformation at contacts → bond formation → decompression with elastic recovery → ejection.

questions.answer:
1. Interparticulate friction: resists rearrangement; reduced by glidants (colloidal silica, talc).
2. Die-wall friction: absorbs applied force, uneven density, high ejection force, sticking/capping; reduced by lubricants — boundary (magnesium stearate, sodium stearyl fumarate) and fluid (stearic acid, hydrogenated oils, PEG).
3. Over-lubrication: hydrophobic film → weaker bonding (plastic materials), slower dissolution.
4. Force balance (single-ended): FA = FL + FD.
5. Force transmission ratio R = FL/FU; example 10.0 kN upper, 8.5 kN lower → R = 0.85, FD = 1.5 kN, mean force 9.25 kN.
6. Radial transmission: K = σradial/σaxial; residual radial pressure governs ejection.
7. Exponential loss: FL = FA e^(−4µKH/D); µ = 0.3, K = 0.4, H/D = 0.4 → FL/FA = 0.83; loss increases with friction and H/D.
8. Density distribution: high-density zones near upper punch edges, low at lower centre in single-ended compression; more symmetric in double-ended (rotary).
9. Measurement: strain gauges (Wheatstone bridge) on punches, eye-bolt, rollers; piezoelectric transducers; instrumented die for radial force; LVDT for displacement; ejection force; compaction simulators.

# Unit 1: Preformulation, stability, pharmaceutical dispersions and parenterals

This unit covers syllabus item 1(a): preformulation concepts, drug–excipient interactions and the methods used to detect them, kinetics of stability and stability testing, theories of dispersion, emulsions, suspensions and SMEDDS, and small and large volume parenterals. At B.Pharm level you learnt *what* preformulation measures; at M.Pharm level the examiner expects *why* each test matters, the mechanism behind each failure, the equations, and the regulatory framework (ICH Q1A(R2), Q1B, Q8–Q10).

## 1.1 Preformulation concepts

**Preformulation** is the investigation of the physical, chemical and biopharmaceutical properties of a drug substance, alone and in combination with excipients, done before formulation development so that a stable, bioavailable and manufacturable dosage form can be designed with the least trial and error.

In modern development it is the first block of **Quality by Design (QbD)**: preformulation data identify the drug's **critical material attributes** (particle size, polymorph, salt form, hygroscopicity, impurity profile) that will later be linked to the **critical quality attributes** of the product.

### Stages and decisions

```text
New drug substance (small quantity, often < 1 g at first)
   │
   ├─ Identity and purity: HPLC, impurity profile, residual solvents
   ├─ Solid state: crystal form, polymorph screen, amorphous content, hydrates
   ├─ Solution properties: pKa, intrinsic solubility, pH–solubility profile, log P / log D
   ├─ Solid and solution stability: pH–rate profile, forced degradation
   ├─ Powder properties: particle size, shape, density, flow, compressibility
   ├─ Biopharmaceutics: permeability (Caco-2), BCS class, dissolution rate
   └─ Compatibility with candidate excipients
   ↓
Decisions: salt / polymorph to develop, dosage form, process (DC vs wet granulation),
excipient short-list, pack, storage conditions, analytical methods
```

### Key parameters and their meaning

| Parameter | Method | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pKa | Potentiometric or UV titration, solubility–pH method | Predicts ionisation, solubility and absorption along the gut (pH-partition) |
| Intrinsic solubility (S0) and pH–solubility | Shake-flask, HPLC assay | S = S0[1 + 10^(pH − pKa)] for a weak acid; decides salt need |
| log P / log D | Shake-flask octanol–water, HPLC retention | Membrane permeability; log D at pH 7.4 is more useful for ionisable drugs |
| Intrinsic dissolution rate | Fixed-area compressed disc (Wood's apparatus) | Rate per cm² independent of particle size; values below about 0.1 mg/cm²/min often mean dissolution-limited absorption |
| Polymorphs, hydrates, amorphous form | DSC, TGA, PXRD, hot-stage microscopy, FTIR/Raman, solid-state NMR | Solubility and stability differ; risk of form change during milling, granulation or storage |
| Hygroscopicity | Dynamic vapour sorption (DVS) | Choice of process, excipients and pack |
| Particle size and shape | Laser diffraction, microscopy | Content uniformity, dissolution, flow |
| Flow and compressibility | Carr's index, Hausner ratio, angle of repose, Heckel analysis | Direct compression versus granulation (see Unit 5–6) |

**BCS (Biopharmaceutics Classification System):** Class I high solubility–high permeability, II low solubility–high permeability, III high solubility–low permeability, IV low–low. "High solubility" means the highest single therapeutic dose dissolves in 250 ml or less of aqueous media over pH 1.2–6.8 at 37 °C (ICH M9). Class II drugs gain most from formulation tools such as salt formation, particle size reduction, solid dispersions and lipid systems such as SMEDDS.

## 1.2 Drug–excipient interactions

An excipient is not inert: it can change the chemical stability, physical form or release of the drug. Interactions are of two kinds.

**Physical interactions** — no new chemical bond, but performance changes:

- Adsorption of the drug on a high-surface excipient (drug on talc, colloidal silica or activated charcoal), lowering dissolution.
- Complexation (tetracycline with calcium or magnesium salts; drugs with cyclodextrins, which may be wanted).
- Change of polymorph or loss of crystallinity during processing with an excipient.
- Eutectic formation, lowering melting point and causing sticking.
- Lubricant film: over-mixed magnesium stearate coats granules and slows dissolution and lowers hardness.

**Chemical interactions** — a new chemical species forms:

| Interaction | Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maillard reaction | Reducing sugar carbonyl + primary or secondary amine → glycosylamine → brown Amadori products | Lactose with amine drugs (for example fluoxetine and amlodipine) |
| Base-catalysed hydrolysis | Alkaline lubricant raises micro-environmental pH | Magnesium stearate with aspirin |
| Oxidation by peroxide impurities | Hydroperoxides in povidone, crospovidone, polysorbates, PEG | Oxidation of drugs with sulphide or amine groups |
| Transesterification / esterification | Ester exchange with PEG or with citric/tartaric acid | Drugs with ester or hydroxyl groups |
| Acid–base reaction | Acidic drug with basic excipient (or reverse) | Salt disproportionation in tablets |
| Reaction with aldehyde impurities | Formaldehyde or furfural traces | Gelatin cross-linking in capsules, slowing dissolution |

**The micro-environmental pH** idea is important: in a solid dosage form the "pH" that matters is that of the thin water layer adsorbed on particles, set mainly by the excipients. That is why a drug stable in a buffered solution may still degrade in a tablet.

### Methods to detect interactions

1. **Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC):** 1:1 physical mixtures of drug and excipient are heated and compared with the pure components. Disappearance or shift of the drug melting peak, new peaks, or changes in enthalpy suggest interaction. Fast, needs milligrams, but a change in DSC may be only a physical (dissolution of drug in a molten excipient) event, so it is a *screen*, not proof.
2. **Isothermal stress testing (IST):** binary mixtures (often with about 5–20% added water) are stored at elevated temperature (for example 40–60 °C) for 1–4 weeks and assayed by HPLC for loss of drug and new degradants. More reliable than DSC because it measures real chemical change.
3. **FTIR / Raman:** shifts or loss of characteristic bands (carbonyl, amine, hydroxyl) indicate bonding or salt formation.
4. **Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD):** detects change of crystal form or loss of crystallinity.
5. **HPLC / LC–MS:** identifies and quantifies degradants, gives kinetic data.
6. **Thermogravimetry (TGA), hot-stage microscopy, solid-state NMR, isothermal microcalorimetry:** microcalorimetry detects very slow reactions at near-ambient temperature from heat flow.
7. **Statistical (factorial) compatibility screens:** instead of one-by-one binary mixtures, a fractional factorial design of prototype mixtures shows which excipient causes the change (see Unit 2).

## 1.3 Kinetics of stability

### Orders of reaction

| Order | Rate law | Integrated form | Half-life | Shelf life (t90) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zero | −dC/dt = k0 | C = C0 − k0t | t½ = C0/(2k0) | t90 = 0.1C0/k0 |
| First | −dC/dt = k1C | ln C = ln C0 − k1t | t½ = 0.693/k1 | t90 = 0.105/k1 |
| Second (equal concentrations) | −dC/dt = k2C² | 1/C = 1/C0 + k2t | t½ = 1/(k2C0) | t90 = 0.11/(k2C0) |

**Apparent (pseudo) zero order:** in a suspension only the dissolved drug degrades, and the solution stays saturated because solid keeps dissolving, so the rate k0 = k1 × Cs is constant until the solid is used up.

**Pseudo-first order:** hydrolysis is truly second order (drug + water) but water is in such excess that its concentration does not change, so the rate looks first order.

### Factors affecting degradation rate

- **pH:** specific acid catalysis (H+), specific base catalysis (OH−) and general acid–base catalysis by buffer species. The observed rate kobs = k0 + kH[H+] + kOH[OH−] + buffer terms. Plotting log kobs against pH gives a **pH–rate profile** (V-shaped, U-shaped, sigmoid or bell-shaped) whose minimum gives the pH of maximum stability for the product.
- **Temperature:** Arrhenius equation (below).
- **Ionic strength:** primary salt effect (Brønsted–Bjerrum): log k = log k0 + 1.02 zAzB√μ in water at 25 °C; ions of like charge react faster at higher ionic strength.
- **Dielectric constant of solvent:** reactions between ions of opposite charge are slowed by raising the dielectric constant.
- **Moisture, oxygen, light, metal ions** (catalysing oxidation) and the excipients described above.

### Arrhenius equation and accelerated prediction

k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), or ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT).

A plot of ln k against 1/T (T in kelvin) is a straight line with slope −Ea/R. Extrapolating to the storage temperature gives k there and hence the predicted shelf life.

**Worked example.** First-order rate constants for a drug in solution were 0.0042 day⁻¹ at 50 °C, 0.0105 day⁻¹ at 60 °C and 0.0250 day⁻¹ at 70 °C. Predict t90 at 25 °C.

| T (°C) | T (K) | 1/T (K⁻¹) | k (day⁻¹) | ln k |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50 | 323.15 | 0.003095 | 0.0042 | −5.473 |
| 60 | 333.15 | 0.003002 | 0.0105 | −4.556 |
| 70 | 343.15 | 0.002914 | 0.0250 | −3.689 |

Least-squares slope = −9,890 K, so Ea = 9,890 × 8.314 = **about 82 kJ/mol**. Intercept ln A = 25.13. At 298.15 K: ln k = 25.13 − 9,890/298.15 = −8.04, so k25 = **3.2 × 10⁻⁴ day⁻¹** and t90 = 0.105/k25 = **about 326 days (just under 11 months)**. The prediction must be confirmed by real-time data, because the mechanism may change with temperature.

**Limitations of accelerated prediction:** valid only if the degradation mechanism and order do not change across the temperature range; not valid for physical changes (melting of a suppository base, protein denaturation, emulsion cracking, polymorph conversion), for evaporative loss, or where moisture content changes with temperature in a solid. Diffusion-controlled solid-state reactions often do not obey Arrhenius behaviour.

**Q10 method** (quick estimate without full data): Q10 = k(T+10)/kT, often taken as 2, 3 or 4. Shelf life at a lower temperature ≈ shelf life at the higher temperature × Q10^(ΔT/10).

## 1.4 Stability testing (ICH Q1A(R2) and related guidelines)

**Stability** is the capacity of a drug product to remain within its specifications of identity, strength, quality and purity throughout its shelf life in the proposed container. Stability testing provides evidence of how quality varies with time under temperature, humidity and light, and fixes the re-test period of the drug substance and the shelf life and storage conditions of the product.

### Types of stability study

- **Stress (forced degradation) testing** on the drug substance: heat, humidity, acid and base hydrolysis, oxidation (for example hydrogen peroxide) and light. Purpose: find degradation pathways and prove that the assay method is **stability-indicating**.
- **Accelerated testing**, **intermediate testing** and **long-term (real-time) testing** on at least three primary batches (pilot scale or larger) in the proposed pack.
- **Photostability testing (ICH Q1B):** overall illumination not less than 1.2 million lux hours and integrated near-UV energy not less than 200 watt-hours/m².
- **In-use stability** (multi-dose products after opening), **ongoing (commitment) stability** on production batches, and stability for post-approval changes.
- **Bracketing and matrixing (ICH Q1D):** reduced designs that test extremes of strength/fill (bracketing) or a planned subset of samples at each time point (matrixing).

### Storage conditions for the general case (ICH Q1A(R2))

| Study | Condition | Minimum period at submission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long term | 25 °C ± 2 °C / 60% RH ± 5% RH **or** 30 °C ± 2 °C / 65% RH ± 5% RH | 12 months |
| Intermediate | 30 °C ± 2 °C / 65% RH ± 5% RH | 6 months |
| Accelerated | 40 °C ± 2 °C / 75% RH ± 5% RH | 6 months |

Intermediate testing is needed only when long term is 25 °C/60% RH and a "significant change" occurs at accelerated conditions. Products for refrigerator storage use 5 °C ± 3 °C long term and 25 °C/60% RH accelerated.

**Climatic zones:** I temperate, II subtropical/Mediterranean, III hot–dry, IVa hot–humid, IVb hot–very humid. India is generally treated as **zone IVb**, for which WHO guidance gives long-term conditions of 30 °C ± 2 °C / 75% RH ± 5% RH. This is why Indian packs often carry "Store below 30 °C".

**Testing frequency (long term):** every 3 months in the first year, every 6 months in the second year and annually after that; accelerated at least 0, 3 and 6 months.

**"Significant change"** for a product includes: 5% change in assay from initial value; any degradant exceeding its acceptance criterion; failure of appearance, physical attributes or functionality tests; failure of pH; failure of dissolution for 12 units.

**Parameters tested:** assay, degradation products, dissolution, appearance, hardness/friability (tablets), moisture, pH, viscosity and redispersibility (liquids), microbial limits, preservative content and preservative efficacy, sterility and particulate matter for injections, container–closure integrity.

**Shelf-life assignment:** the time at which the one-sided 95% confidence limit of the mean degradation curve meets the specification limit (ICH Q1E statistical evaluation). Limited extrapolation beyond real-time data is allowed only when supported by accelerated data.

## 1.5 Theories of dispersion

A **dispersion** is a system in which one phase (dispersed phase) is distributed as particles or droplets through another (continuous phase or dispersion medium). Suspensions (solid in liquid, particles usually above about 1 µm) and emulsions (liquid in liquid) are **coarse dispersions**; they are thermodynamically unstable because they have a large interfacial area and therefore a high interfacial free energy: ΔG = γ·ΔA.

### Theories of emulsification

1. **Surface (interfacial) tension theory:** emulsifiers lower the interfacial tension γ, so less work (γΔA) is needed to create the droplet surface, and coalescence has a smaller driving force.
2. **Oriented wedge theory:** emulsifier molecules orient at the interface with their hydrophilic end in water and lipophilic end in oil; the bulkier, more soluble end lies in the continuous phase, curving the film. Monovalent soaps (sodium oleate) favour o/w; divalent soaps (calcium oleate, two hydrocarbon chains) favour w/o.
3. **Interfacial film theory:** the emulsifier forms a barrier film around each droplet. Types of film:
   - **Monomolecular film** — surfactants (Tweens, Spans, sodium lauryl sulphate); a mixture of a water-soluble and an oil-soluble surfactant packs more tightly (complex film).
   - **Multimolecular film** — hydrophilic colloids (acacia, gelatin) form a thick, viscous film that resists coalescence mechanically.
   - **Solid particle film** — finely divided solids (bentonite, aluminium hydroxide) wetted by both phases collect at the interface (Pickering emulsions); the phase that wets the solid better becomes the continuous phase.
4. **Electrical double layer and DLVO theory:** charged droplets or particles repel; stability results from the balance of van der Waals attraction and electrostatic repulsion.

### DLVO theory (Derjaguin–Landau–Verwey–Overbeek)

Total potential energy of interaction VT = VA + VR, where VA (attraction) falls off with distance and VR (repulsion) depends on the surface potential and the thickness of the double layer (1/κ, which shrinks as electrolyte is added).

```text
Potential energy
  ↑            ___  primary maximum (energy barrier)
  |           /   \
  |          /     \______________
  |---------/------------\____/------→ distance between particles
  |        |              secondary minimum (loose, reversible flocs)
  |        |
  ↓   primary minimum (close contact: irreversible aggregation / caking)
```

- A high primary maximum keeps particles apart (deflocculated).
- Particles caught in the **secondary minimum** form loose flocs that redisperse easily — the basis of **controlled flocculation**.
- Electrolyte compresses the double layer, lowers the barrier and favours flocculation (Schulze–Hardy rule: flocculating power rises steeply with counter-ion valency).
- **Steric stabilisation** by adsorbed polymers or non-ionic surfactants adds a non-electrostatic repulsion, useful in high-ionic-strength products.

### Zeta potential

The potential at the shear plane between the fixed (Stern) layer and the mobile diffuse layer, measured from electrophoretic mobility. High magnitude (often quoted as beyond about ±30 mV) means a deflocculated, electrostatically stable system; lowering it to a small value with electrolytes produces controlled flocculation.

## 1.6 Suspensions: preparation and stability

**Stokes' law:** v = d²(ρs − ρo)g / 18η

**Worked example:** particles of 10 µm diameter (d = 10⁻³ cm), density 1.3 g/cm³, in water (1.0 g/cm³, η = 0.01 poise): v = (10⁻³)² × 0.3 × 981 / (18 × 0.01) = 1.6 × 10⁻³ cm/s ≈ 5.9 cm per hour. Raising the vehicle viscosity to 5 cP (0.05 poise) cuts this to about 1.2 cm per hour. Halving particle size cuts velocity four-fold.

### Flocculated versus deflocculated suspensions

| Property | Deflocculated | Flocculated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Particles | Separate | Loose aggregates (flocs) |
| Sedimentation rate | Slow | Fast |
| Sediment | Closely packed, may form a cake | Loose, large volume, easily redispersed |
| Supernatant | Cloudy | Clear |
| Appearance | Elegant for longer | Less elegant |

**Approach used in practice:** controlled flocculation with electrolytes, surfactants or polymers, then a **structured vehicle** (suspending agents such as methylcellulose, sodium CMC, xanthan gum, bentonite, carbomer — pseudoplastic or thixotropic) to slow settling of the flocs.

**Evaluation parameters:**

- Sedimentation volume F = Vu/V0 (ultimate sediment volume ÷ original suspension volume). Example: 45 ml sediment in a 50 ml suspension gives F = 0.9.
- Degree of flocculation β = F/F∞, where F∞ is the sedimentation volume of the deflocculated system.
- Redispersibility (number of inversions), rheology, zeta potential, particle size growth (Ostwald ripening, crystal growth, polymorphic change), drug content uniformity on shaking.

**Preparation:** wetting of hydrophobic powder with a wetting agent or glycerin (levigation), dispersion of suspending agent, mixing, homogenisation or colloid milling, controlled flocculation, final volume. Large-scale: precipitation methods (solvent change, pH change, double decomposition) can also produce fine particles.

## 1.7 Emulsions: preparation and stability

**Choice of emulsifier — HLB system.** HLB 3–6 favours w/o, 8–18 favours o/w. Each oil has a "required HLB" for an o/w emulsion. A blend of two surfactants gives HLB = f × HLB_A + (1 − f) × HLB_B.

**Worked example:** required HLB 12 using Tween 80 (HLB 15.0) and Span 80 (HLB 4.3): f(Tween) = (12 − 4.3)/(15.0 − 4.3) = 0.72, so about **72% Tween 80 and 28% Span 80** by weight of the emulsifier blend.

**Preparation methods:** dry gum (continental, 4:2:1 oil:water:gum for fixed oils), wet gum (English), bottle method (volatile oils), in-situ soap method, and at industrial scale phase inversion and high-pressure homogenisation or microfluidisation.

**Instabilities:**

| Instability | Reversible? | Cause and control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Creaming / sedimentation | Yes | Density difference, large droplets; reduce droplet size, raise viscosity, match densities |
| Flocculation | Usually yes | Weak attraction; control zeta potential |
| Coalescence → cracking (breaking) | No | Film rupture; adequate emulsifier, avoid incompatible additives, temperature extremes, microbial attack |
| Ostwald ripening | No | Small droplets dissolve into large ones (higher solubility of small droplets); add a poorly water-soluble oil |
| Phase inversion | — | o/w changes to w/o on changing phase volume ratio (above about 74% internal phase), temperature (PIT for non-ionic surfactants) or adding a divalent ion |

**Evaluation:** droplet size distribution (microscopy, laser diffraction), zeta potential, viscosity, phase separation after centrifugation, freeze–thaw cycling, conductivity (to identify o/w), dilution and dye tests.

## 1.8 Self-micro-emulsifying drug delivery systems (SMEDDS)

**SMEDDS** are isotropic mixtures of oil, surfactant (usually non-ionic with HLB above about 12) and co-surfactant or co-solvent, containing the dissolved drug, which form a fine oil-in-water micro-emulsion spontaneously on gentle agitation in aqueous media such as gastrointestinal fluid. Droplets are typically below about 100 nm for SMEDDS; coarser systems (roughly 100–300 nm) are called SEDDS, and nano-sized ones are often called SNEDDS.

**Why they improve absorption of BCS class II drugs:** the drug stays in solution; huge interfacial area for partition; lipid digestion products form mixed micelles with bile; lymphatic transport of highly lipophilic drugs can bypass first-pass metabolism; some surfactants inhibit P-glycoprotein efflux.

**Components:**

| Component | Examples | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oil | Medium-chain triglycerides, mono- and diglycerides, oleic acid, vegetable oils | Solubilises the lipophilic drug; promotes lymphatic transport (long-chain) |
| Surfactant | Polysorbate 80, polyoxyl 35 or 40 castor oil, caprylocaproyl macrogolglycerides | Lowers interfacial tension, enables spontaneous emulsification |
| Co-surfactant / co-solvent | Transcutol (diethylene glycol monoethyl ether), propylene glycol, PEG 400, ethanol | Increases interfacial fluidity and drug load |

**Pouton's lipid formulation classification:** Type I oils only (need digestion); Type II oils + water-insoluble surfactants (SEDDS); Type IIIA/IIIB oils + water-soluble surfactants ± co-solvents (SMEDDS; IIIB has less oil); Type IV surfactants and co-solvents without oil (risk of drug precipitation on dilution).

**Development:** solubility of drug in each excipient → construct **pseudo-ternary phase diagrams** (oil vs surfactant:co-surfactant mixture vs water, titration method) to find the micro-emulsion region → select ratios → load drug → optimise by DoE (Unit 2).

**Evaluation:** self-emulsification time and grade, droplet size and polydispersity (dynamic light scattering), zeta potential, robustness to dilution (50–1000 times, different media), cloud point, thermodynamic stability (heating–cooling cycles, centrifugation, freeze–thaw), drug precipitation on dilution, in-vitro dissolution and lipolysis testing, transmittance.

**Solid SMEDDS:** liquid SMEDDS adsorbed on porous carriers (colloidal silica, magnesium aluminometasilicate), spray-dried, or filled in hard or soft gelatin capsules; improves handling and stability.

**Limitations:** chemical instability of drug in lipid, high surfactant content (GI irritation), capsule shell interaction, precipitation on dilution (overcome by supersaturable SMEDDS with polymeric precipitation inhibitors such as HPMC).

## 1.9 Large and small volume parenterals

**Parenteral preparations** are sterile preparations intended for administration by injection, infusion or implantation into the body. By USP convention, a **small-volume parenteral (SVP)** has 100 ml or less per container and a **large-volume parenteral (LVP)** is a single-dose infusion of more than 100 ml (pharmacopoeias word this slightly differently).

### Physiological considerations

- **Route:** intravenous (no absorption phase, any volume as infusion but no oily or suspended particles), intramuscular, subcutaneous (limited volume, suspensions and oils possible), intradermal, intrathecal and intra-ocular (no preservative, strict isotonicity).
- **Tonicity and osmolarity:** plasma osmolality is about 285–295 mOsm/kg. 0.9% NaCl gives about 308 mOsm/L (9 g/L ÷ 58.44 × 2); 5% glucose about 278 mOsm/L. Hypotonic solutions given IV can cause haemolysis; hypertonic solutions are given slowly into large veins (parenteral nutrition through a central line).
- **pH:** blood pH 7.35–7.45 with good buffer capacity, so small volumes away from 7.4 are tolerated; LVPs should be close to physiological pH and lightly buffered. Pain, phlebitis and tissue damage increase at extreme pH.
- **Pyrogens/endotoxins, particulate matter** (emboli, granulomas), **sterility**, **volume and rate** of infusion.

### Formulation considerations

| Component | Examples and remarks |
| --- | --- |
| Vehicle | Water for Injections (WFI); non-aqueous: fixed oils (sesame, cotton-seed), ethyl oleate, benzyl benzoate (IM only); water-miscible co-solvents: ethanol, propylene glycol, PEG 300/400, glycerin |
| Solubilisers | Polysorbate 80, polyoxyl castor oil, cyclodextrins (hydroxypropyl-β-, sulfobutylether-β-) |
| Buffers | Phosphate, citrate, acetate |
| Antioxidants | Sodium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, ascorbic acid; nitrogen flushing of headspace |
| Chelating agents | Disodium edetate |
| Preservatives | Benzyl alcohol, chlorocresol, phenol, parabens — for multi-dose SVPs only; **not** in LVPs or in intrathecal, intracisternal and intra-ocular products |
| Tonicity adjusters | Sodium chloride, dextrose, mannitol |
| Bulking agents and cryoprotectants (freeze-dried) | Mannitol, sucrose, trehalose, glycine |

LVPs: simple solutions (electrolytes, dextrose, amino acids, lipid emulsions for parenteral nutrition), no preservative, single dose, usually terminally sterilised in flexible bags or glass bottles.

### Manufacturing

```text
Water for Injections (distillation or equivalent) → compounding in clean area (grade C/D)
→ filtration (0.22 µm sterilising grade filter, integrity tested: bubble point / pressure hold)
→ filling and sealing in grade A zone with grade B background (aseptic) or grade C for
  products to be terminally sterilised → terminal sterilisation (moist heat, typically
  121 °C for at least 15 min equivalent; F0 used to express lethality)
→ leak test → visual inspection → labelling and packing → QC release
```

- **Clean rooms:** graded A to D (Schedule M / EU GMP Annex 1), with HEPA-filtered air, pressure differentials, airlocks and environmental monitoring of viable and non-viable particles.
- **Terminal sterilisation** is preferred whenever the product can withstand it; it gives a sterility assurance level (SAL) of 10⁻⁶. **Aseptic processing** is used for heat-labile products and is validated by media fills (process simulation).
- **Freeze-drying (lyophilisation)** for unstable drugs: freezing below the collapse/eutectic temperature, primary drying (sublimation under vacuum), secondary drying (desorption).
- **Containers:** Type I borosilicate glass for most injections; Type II (treated soda-lime) for some neutral/acidic aqueous products; Type III for non-aqueous; plastics (PVC, polyolefin bags) for LVPs; rubber closures tested for extractables.

### Evaluation (quality control)

- **Sterility test** (membrane filtration or direct inoculation; fluid thioglycollate medium at 30–35 °C and soya-bean casein digest medium at 20–25 °C for 14 days).
- **Bacterial endotoxins test** (LAL: gel-clot, turbidimetric, chromogenic) or the rabbit pyrogen test.
- **Particulate matter:** light obscuration — LVP not more than 25 particles/ml ≥ 10 µm and 3 particles/ml ≥ 25 µm; SVP not more than 6,000 per container ≥ 10 µm and 600 per container ≥ 25 µm.
- **Visible particles and clarity** (inspection against black and white backgrounds), **leaker test** (dye bath with methylene blue under vacuum for ampoules; container closure integrity for vials), **extractable volume**, **pH**, **osmolality**, assay and impurities, **uniformity of content** for powders.

## Remember

- Preformulation feeds QbD: critical material attributes found here are linked to product CQAs later.
- Drug–excipient screens: DSC is a fast screen; isothermal stress testing with HPLC confirms; know Maillard reaction (lactose + amine) and magnesium stearate–aspirin.
- First-order t90 = 0.105/k; Arrhenius slope = −Ea/R; worked example gave Ea ≈ 82 kJ/mol and t90 ≈ 326 days at 25 °C.
- ICH Q1A(R2): long term 25/60 or 30/65 (12 months), intermediate 30/65, accelerated 40/75 (6 months); India is zone IVb (30 °C/75% RH); Q1B photostability 1.2 million lux h and 200 W·h/m².
- DLVO: VT = VA + VR; secondary minimum = loose flocs (controlled flocculation); zeta potential governs.
- F = Vu/V0; β = F/F∞; Stokes velocity ∝ d².
- SMEDDS: oil + surfactant (HLB > 12) + co-surfactant; droplets < 100 nm; Pouton types I–IV; pseudo-ternary phase diagrams.
- SVP ≤ 100 ml, LVP > 100 ml (USP); LVPs have no preservative; 0.9% NaCl ≈ 308 mOsm/L.

# Unit 2: Optimization techniques and design of experiments

This unit covers syllabus item 1(b): the concept and parameters of optimization, optimization techniques in pharmaceutical formulation and processing, statistical design, response surface methodology, contour plots, factorial designs and their application in formulation. It links directly to QbD (ICH Q8(R2)), where design of experiments (DoE) is the tool that builds the **design space**.

## 2.1 Concept of optimization

**Optimization** means finding the best possible composition or process conditions for a product, within the given constraints, so that one or more responses (dissolution, hardness, entrapment, particle size) reach their desired values.

The traditional approach, **one factor at a time (OFAT)** — change one variable while holding others fixed — has serious drawbacks:

- It cannot detect **interactions** (for example, the effect of binder level on hardness may depend on compression force).
- It needs many experiments for limited information and may miss the true optimum, which can lie in a region never tested.
- It gives no predictive model, so the formulator cannot say what will happen between tested points.

Statistical optimization varies all factors together according to a planned design, fits a mathematical model, and uses the model to predict and locate the optimum with a known uncertainty.

## 2.2 Terms and parameters of optimization

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Factor (independent variable) | Input the formulator controls | Polymer %, compression force, stirring speed |
| Level | Value at which a factor is set | Low (−1), centre (0), high (+1) |
| Response (dependent variable) | Measured output | % drug released at 8 h, hardness, particle size |
| Quantitative factor | Measured on a numeric scale | Binder concentration |
| Qualitative (categorical) factor | Type, not amount | Type of binder (PVP or starch paste), type of mixer |
| Effect | Change in response caused by changing a factor from low to high level | Main effect of A |
| Interaction | Effect of one factor depends on the level of another | AB |
| Coded value | Actual value scaled to −1 … +1 | X = (actual − centre)/half-range |
| Constraint | Limit the solution must meet | Hardness ≥ 5 kg, friability < 1% |
| Confounding (aliasing) | Two effects cannot be separated in a reduced design | In a half-fraction 2³⁻¹, C aliased with AB |
| Replication | Repeating runs to estimate pure error | Centre point repeated 3–5 times |
| Randomisation | Running trials in random order | Protects against drift and time effects |
| Blocking | Grouping runs to remove a known nuisance source | Two batches of raw material |

**Optimization parameters** are classified as:

- **Problem type: constrained versus unconstrained.** Real pharmaceutical problems are constrained (for example "maximise dissolution while hardness stays above 5 kg").
- **Variables: independent (formulation and process) and dependent (responses).**
- **Single-response versus multiple-response.** Multiple responses need trade-off tools such as the **desirability function** (each response converted to a 0–1 scale; overall D is the geometric mean, and the optimum maximises D) or overlay of contour plots.

## 2.3 Classification of optimization techniques

```text
Optimization techniques
├─ Classical (calculus based) — differentiate a known equation, set derivative = 0;
│                               works only for simple single-response problems
├─ Statistical design (DoE) — experiments first, then model
│   ├─ Screening designs: Plackett–Burman, fractional factorial, Taguchi
│   ├─ Factorial designs: full 2^k, 3^k, mixed-level
│   ├─ Response surface designs: central composite, Box–Behnken, 3^k
│   └─ Mixture designs: simplex lattice, simplex centroid, extreme vertices
├─ Model-free / sequential search: EVOP, simplex method (Spendley), steepest ascent
└─ Computer search methods: grid search, Lagrangian method, canonical analysis,
   artificial neural networks, genetic algorithms
```

### Sequential (search) methods

- **Evolutionary operation (EVOP):** small deliberate changes are made to a running production process (usually a 2² design around the current set point), repeated many times; when a change shows a real improvement the set point is moved. Safe because changes are too small to make out-of-specification product. Suited to production, not development.
- **Simplex method:** a geometric figure with k + 1 vertices for k factors (triangle for two factors). The worst vertex is reflected through the centroid of the others, and the simplex "walks" towards the optimum. The modified (Nelder–Mead) simplex can expand or contract.

### Lagrangian method

Used when the response and constraint can be written as equations (from a fitted model). The objective function and the constraints are combined with a Lagrange multiplier λ and the partial derivatives are set to zero. A classical example is optimizing tablet dissolution subject to a hardness constraint.

### Search (grid) method

The fitted model is evaluated at a fine grid of combinations; all combinations that meet the constraints are listed and the best is chosen. With a computer it handles many responses and constraints and does not need differentiable equations.

## 2.4 Statistical designs

### Screening designs

Used early, when there are many factors (say 6–15) and the aim is only to find the few important ones.

- **Plackett–Burman designs:** N runs (a multiple of 4) screen up to N − 1 factors at two levels; main effects only, interactions assumed negligible. For example 12 runs for up to 11 factors.
- **Fractional factorial (2^(k−p)):** a fraction of the full factorial. The **resolution** tells what is aliased: resolution III — main effects aliased with two-factor interactions; resolution IV — main effects clear, two-factor interactions aliased with each other; resolution V — main effects and two-factor interactions clear.
- **Taguchi orthogonal arrays** (L4, L8, L9, L18): also aim at **robustness** — choosing settings that make the product insensitive to noise factors, using signal-to-noise ratios.

### Full factorial designs

All combinations of all levels. For k factors at 2 levels: **2^k runs**; at 3 levels: **3^k runs** (3² = 9, 3³ = 27).

**2² design with interaction model:** Y = b0 + b1X1 + b2X2 + b12X1X2.

**2^k design** fits a linear model with interactions but cannot detect curvature; adding **centre points** tests for curvature and gives pure error.

### Response surface designs

To fit a **second-order (quadratic) model**:

Y = b0 + b1X1 + b2X2 + b12X1X2 + b11X1² + b22X2²

each factor needs at least three levels.

- **Central composite design (CCD):** a 2^k factorial (or fraction) + 2k **axial (star) points** at ±α + several **centre points**. Runs = 2^k + 2k + n0; for two factors with five centre points, 4 + 4 + 5 = 13 runs. α = (2^k)^(1/4) makes the design **rotatable** (equal prediction variance at equal distance from the centre): 1.414 for k = 2, 1.682 for k = 3. α = 1 gives a **face-centred CCD**, with only three levels per factor.
- **Box–Behnken design (BBD):** three levels per factor, points at the mid-points of the cube edges plus centre points; no runs at the extreme corners (useful when all-high or all-low combinations are impossible or unsafe). Three factors: 12 + centre points (commonly 3) = 15 runs; four factors: 24 + 3 = 27 runs.
- **3^k full factorial:** 9 runs for two factors; becomes large quickly.

### Mixture designs

When factors are proportions of a whole that must sum to 1 (for example the oil : surfactant : co-surfactant ratio of a SMEDDS, or a blend of three fillers), the factors are not independent, so ordinary factorial designs cannot be used.

- **Simplex lattice {q, m}:** q components, proportions in steps of 1/m. A {3, 2} lattice has 6 points: three pure components and three 50:50 binary blends.
- **Simplex centroid:** adds the centroid (1/3 : 1/3 : 1/3) and similar blends; 7 points for 3 components.
- **Extreme vertices design:** used when components have lower and upper limits (constrained mixture region).
- The model is the **Scheffé polynomial**, for example Y = b1X1 + b2X2 + b3X3 + b12X1X2 + b13X1X3 + b23X2X3 (no intercept).

## 2.5 Calculating effects in a 2³ factorial design (worked example)

A tablet was studied with factor A = binder concentration, B = superdisintegrant concentration, C = compression force, each at two levels (coded −1 and +1). Response: disintegration time (min).

| Run (Yates order) | A | B | C | Disintegration time (min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) | − | − | − | 4.2 |
| a | + | − | − | 7.8 |
| b | − | + | − | 2.6 |
| ab | + | + | − | 5.0 |
| c | − | − | + | 5.9 |
| ac | + | − | + | 10.1 |
| bc | − | + | + | 3.7 |
| abc | + | + | + | 7.3 |

**Rule:** effect of a factor = (sum of responses where the column sign is +) − (sum where it is −), divided by 2^(k−1) = 4. The sign column for an interaction is the product of the parent columns.

Main effect of A = [(7.8 + 5.0 + 10.1 + 7.3) − (4.2 + 2.6 + 5.9 + 3.7)] / 4 = (30.2 − 16.4)/4 = **3.45 min**.

| Effect | Value (min) | Regression coefficient (= effect/2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mean (b0) | 5.825 | 5.825 |
| A (binder) | +3.45 | +1.725 |
| B (disintegrant) | −2.35 | −1.175 |
| C (force) | +1.85 | +0.925 |
| AB | −0.45 | −0.225 |
| AC | +0.45 | +0.225 |
| BC | −0.15 | −0.075 |
| ABC | +0.15 | +0.075 |

**Interpretation:**

- Binder level has the largest effect: raising it lengthens disintegration by 3.45 min on average.
- Superdisintegrant shortens it by 2.35 min; higher force lengthens it by 1.85 min.
- Interactions are small; AB negative means the disintegrant partly offsets the binder effect at high binder level.
- The model (ignoring the three-factor term) is Y = 5.825 + 1.725A − 1.175B + 0.925C − 0.225AB + 0.225AC − 0.075BC. Predicted disintegration at A = −1, B = +1, C = −1 is 2.53 min (observed 2.6 min).

Which effects are real? Without replicates, use a **half-normal (or normal) probability plot** of effects: real effects fall off the straight line formed by the small (noise) effects. With replicates or centre points, test each effect by ANOVA or a t-test against the error (Unit 6).

**Yates' algorithm** gives the same effects by repeated pairwise sums and differences of the responses arranged in standard order — handy without software.

## 2.6 Response surface method and contour plots

**Response surface methodology (RSM)** is a collection of statistical and mathematical techniques used to model and analyse problems in which a response is influenced by several variables, with the aim of optimizing that response. Steps:

1. Choose factors (from screening) and ranges; choose a design (CCD, BBD).
2. Run experiments in random order; measure responses.
3. Fit a polynomial model by multiple linear regression; check it by ANOVA: significant model, non-significant **lack of fit**, high R² with adjusted R² and predicted R² in reasonable agreement, adequate precision; check residual plots.
4. Draw **response surface (3-D)** and **contour (2-D)** plots.
5. Find the optimum (numerical optimization, desirability, or overlay of contour plots).
6. **Check-point (validation) batches:** prepare 2–3 batches at the predicted optimum and compare observed with predicted responses; a small percentage prediction error confirms the model.

**Contour plot:** a 2-D graph with two factors on the axes and lines joining combinations that give the same response (like height lines on a map). Straight parallel lines mean no interaction; curved lines mean interaction or quadratic terms; closed ellipses show a maximum or minimum inside the region (a stationary point); a saddle shape shows a minimax.

**Overlay plot:** contour plots of several responses are superimposed and the region meeting every constraint is shaded — this is the operational **design space** (or "sweet spot").

### Worked example: 2² design for a matrix tablet

Factors: X1 = HPMC (coded −1 = 10%, +1 = 20% of tablet weight), X2 = lactose : microcrystalline cellulose ratio (coded). Response: % drug released at 8 h.

| X1 | X2 | Released at 8 h (%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| −1 | −1 | 92 |
| +1 | −1 | 68 |
| −1 | +1 | 96 |
| +1 | +1 | 80 |

b0 = (92 + 68 + 96 + 80)/4 = 84; b1 = (−92 + 68 − 96 + 80)/4 = −10; b2 = (−92 − 68 + 96 + 80)/4 = +4; b12 = (92 − 68 − 96 + 80)/4 = +2.

Model: **Y = 84 − 10X1 + 4X2 + 2X1X2**.

- Target 85% release with X2 = 0: 85 = 84 − 10X1, so X1 = −0.1, i.e. HPMC = 15 + 5 × (−0.1) = **14.5%**.
- The 80% contour passes through (X1, X2) = (0.0, −1), (0.4, 0) and (1.0, +1) — a curved line, because of the interaction term.

Because a 2² design has no curvature terms, the predicted optimum should be confirmed by check-point batches or by adding centre and axial points (moving to a CCD).

## 2.7 Applications of optimization in pharmaceutical formulation and processing

| Area | Typical factors | Typical responses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate-release tablets | Binder, disintegrant, lubricant level, force | Hardness, friability, disintegration, dissolution |
| Matrix sustained-release tablets | Polymer level and viscosity grade, filler type | Release at fixed times, release exponent n, f2 against target |
| Granulation | Binder volume, impeller speed, wet-massing time | Granule size, density, flow |
| Coating | Spray rate, inlet temperature, atomisation pressure | Coating efficiency, film defects, lag time |
| Microspheres / nanoparticles | Polymer:drug ratio, stirring speed, surfactant level | Particle size, entrapment efficiency, release |
| SMEDDS, nanoemulsions | Oil, surfactant, co-surfactant proportions (mixture design) | Droplet size, emulsification time, drug load |
| Liposomes | Lipid:cholesterol ratio, hydration time, sonication | Size, entrapment, zeta potential |
| Analytical methods (AQbD) | Mobile phase pH, organic %, flow rate, column temperature | Resolution, tailing, retention time |
| Process scale-up and robustness | Process parameters around the set point | Robustness of CQAs |

## 2.8 Optimization in Quality by Design

DoE is the link between the steps of QbD (ICH Q8(R2)):

```text
QTPP (quality target product profile)
  → CQAs (critical quality attributes)
  → risk assessment (ICH Q9: fishbone, FMEA) to pick likely CMAs and CPPs
  → screening DoE (Plackett–Burman / fractional factorial)
  → optimization DoE (CCD / BBD / mixture) → models
  → design space (overlay of acceptable regions; movement inside it is not a
    regulatory change)
  → control strategy → continual improvement (ICH Q10)
```

**Software** commonly used: Design-Expert, Minitab, JMP, Statistica, MODDE.

**Advantages of statistical optimization:** fewer experiments for more information; interactions and curvature detected; predictive models; documented scientific basis acceptable to regulators; robust products. **Limitations:** model valid only inside the studied region; poorly chosen ranges or responses give misleading optima; needs statistical skill; qualitative factors complicate RSM.

## Remember

- OFAT misses interactions; DoE varies all factors together and builds a model.
- Runs: 2^k full factorial; CCD = 2^k + 2k + n0 (13 for k = 2 with 5 centre points); rotatable α = (2^k)^¼ (1.414 for k = 2); BBD 15 runs for 3 factors.
- Effect = (Σ+ − Σ−)/2^(k−1); coefficient = effect/2. Worked 2³ example: A +3.45, B −2.35, C +1.85, AB −0.45 min.
- 2² example model Y = 84 − 10X1 + 4X2 + 2X1X2; 85% release needs HPMC 14.5% at X2 = 0.
- Screening: Plackett–Burman, fractional factorial (resolution III/IV/V), Taguchi. Optimization: CCD, BBD, 3^k. Mixtures: simplex lattice/centroid with Scheffé model.
- Validate with check-point batches; check lack of fit, R², adjusted and predicted R².
- Contour lines curved → interaction; overlay plot → design space; desirability 0–1 for many responses.
